utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we start with everything else, just to place on the record that Judge Orie is not able to sit with us for urgent personal matters, and Judge Fluegge and I have agreed that it is in the interests of justice to carry on with the case without his presence. We have been told that the Defence has a preliminary matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] My mike was not switched on. I will repeat myself. Good morning, Mr. Kolenda. Mr. Kolenda, just to remind you that you're still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kolenda. Mr. Kolenda, I want to take you to paragraph 40 of your statement in which you explain that in the morning of 8 June 1993 all the Bosnian Croat men were separated from the civilians and that everybody's personal details were recorded. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it also correct, but unmentioned in your statement, that those people who had fled the area using a vehicle were ordered to hand in their vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall having said that. The civilians for the most part remained in the vehicles. Some people arrived in Galica in their own vehicles, others came by buses and trucks owned by socially owned enterprises, whereas yet another group came on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me take you back to your SIS statement, which we looked at yesterday and which is Exhibit P7092.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we could have that on the screen, please. And I would like to look at page number 8 of that statement for both the B/C/S and the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the version in Croatian be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kolenda, I would like to refer you to a sentence which is in your -- from the top, somewhere around line number 11, and I'll read out that sentence as well -- well, maybe the sentence before as well. It reads as follows: "On 8 June 1993 at 8.00 all men from 50 to 60 years of age were requested to come. They were separated from the civilians and their data were taken. At the same time, all socially owned vehicles and better," as stated, probably refers to better quality, "better private vehicles were also confiscated." So is this --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Namely, the buses we came in were socially owned, and I think even a fire truck was commandeered. When I said private vehicle, I had in mind one vehicle specifically whose owner complained to me. He had bought a stolen off-road vehicle and did not have appropriate documentation for it, I think it was some kind of jeep, and the gentleman's last name was Paklarcic. In the end, the vehicle was seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying that these -- but you're saying that these socially -- these buses and the fire trucks, those vehicles were confiscated? Is that how I understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. And who confiscated these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you stated yesterday, you initially tried to get the help from UNPROFOR in the evacuation of the Bosnian Croat civilians from Travnik but they refused to assist. In paragraph 25 of your statement, you said that UNPROFOR refused because they did not want to take part in ethnic cleansing. Is that correct? Was that the reason why they didn't want to help?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided this statement -- part of the statement based on the information given to me by Mr. Bilandzija and Mr. Leutar because the two of them participated directly in talks with UNPROFOR. They asked that the civilians and the wounded be removed from the western part of Travnik to the eastern part in Nova Bila where a hospital was located; however, UNPROFOR refused, justifying it by saying that they would be committing ethnic cleansing. However, in another instance, he did exactly the opposite. When the Muslim forces in the village of Guca Gora in Travnik surrounded Croat civilians who were in a monastery, for the first time in that war UNPROFOR opened fire at the Muslim forces in order to protect the Croatian civilians. Then UNPROFOR had them evacuated to the area of Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you then tried to obtain the assistance of the Serb counterparts when UNPROFOR didn't want to help in the evacuation of the Bosnian Croat civilians, is it correct that they -- that the Serbs first wanted to consult with their superiors before anything could be agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because they immediately said as far as civilians and the wounded are concerned that there were no problems. They also included children. However, they said that there might be problems with conscripts and military-aged men, the fighters and policemen who were in greater numbers. In that case, they would have to consult the corps concerning our requests in terms of some military issues such as weapons and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution have P3683 on the screen, please. P03683.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, it's appearing on the screen, and I hope it's big enough for you to read. This is an order from General Mladic addressed to the 1st Krajina Corps and it's dated 7th of June, 1993, and in this order he gives instructions on the treatment of the HVO members and the Croatian civilian population in Travnik. Now, if we look at the paragraph under number 1, I'll read that paragraph out, it reads: "With the engagement of the MKCK," which seems to be the Bosnian Serb acronym for International Committee of the Red Cross, "an adequate number of motor vehicles, also to be regulated through the MKCK, drive the civilian population and persons not fit for combat to the sector of Novska in Croatian territory." Sir, were you aware that the evacuation of the Bosnian Croats from Travnik, which UNPROFOR did not want to participate in as they considered it ethnic cleansing, was eventually ordered by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately how many Bosnian Croat civilians from Travnik were evacuated to Novska in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are going about it in a mathematical way, there were between 4- and 5.000 civilians in front of the church and another 1.000 people who were military conscripts, so let's say 5- to 6.000. However, during the evacuation more people came in from different areas. In any case, I think there may have been between 5- and 6.000 people who went from west Travnik to the area of Vlasic. Some 880 of them were military conscripts. There were military-aged men who were taken to Manjaca which would leave between five- and five-and-a-half-thousand people who were supposed to be transported to Novska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you know, when these civilians who ended up in Novska, where they eventually ended up?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it because I was at Manjaca there. When the journalists came to Manjaca on the 10th to see what the conditions of accommodation and our stay there were, a Spanish lady journalist when interviewing me told me that she was happy to be able to tell me that the civilians had already been evacuated from the Vlasic plateau via Novska to Croatia. According to something I learned later, a part of them ended up in southern Herzegovina in the area of Ljubusko and Capljina, whereas another group ended up in Croatia in the area of Orebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look now in the same documents under item number 5, I think you have it on the screen but maybe the English version can -- can move to the next page, and I will read that paragraph out to you as well. Paragraph 5 reads: "As soon as possible take over all the positions that were held by the HVO members that are tactically good for us and help ameliorate our position on the front because we have intelligence that the Muslim sides intends to do the same." Sir, is it not true that the VRS did not assist the HVO out of altruistic motives but that the VRS effectively ameliorated their military positions on the front lines in Central Bosnia by their assistance?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to respond to that question about what the VRS and its command had in mind. I don't know that. How -- obviously they had an interest. Now, as for what kind of interest it was, whether it was tackle positions or promoting an image of being based -- of their actions being based on humanitarian grounds, that's something I cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I just want to ask, sir, do you know what became of the 880 prisoners that went to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, I was one of them. We were put in groups and taken from the area of Vlasic onboard trucks to Manjaca. Once there, we were placed in a collection centre in two rooms. Before the war, they had been stables for cattle. We had them cleaned up and organised things for the best way -- the best life possible. We constructed wooden toilets, we cleaned up the area, and we spent between three and four days. At the outset, we didn't know how long we would need to stay there. We were surrounded by the military police of the VRS who stood guard in the outer parameter beyond the fence and occasionally their patrols came in to check our situation. We received regular meals, provided by the Caritas and the VRS, at least to the amount that was necessary for normal life. We were all exchanged and we left Manjaca for Sokolac. In the village of Brgule we were exchanged. It is in the area of Vares. I have to say that our weapons followed us, without ammunition, though. As I could see later from the documents of the HVO military intelligence service, it had been agreed at the level of commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Finally, how long did you stay at Manjaca for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three and a half or four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between the 8th and the 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have 65 ter 00925 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, what we have in front of us now is an another order from General Mladic issued a few weeks later on the 24th of June, 1993, and it's addressed to the various VRS corps commands. In this order General Mladic, based on his experience with the evacuation of the operation in Travnik, he discusses VRS co-operation with the HVO and gives some very specific instructions to his corps commands on how to approach such co-operation. Before giving his instructions, General Mladic first makes some general remarks about the Croats and Muslims, and I'd like to read out his comments to you. Starting from the last part of the fourth paragraph, General Mladic says: "The Croats have gone from being Muslim allies to being their enemy and are now just trying to save their own population via Republika Srpska. They are counting on their success in the belief that we Serbs are gullible, a view based on historical experience. "In all future talks with Muslims and Croat, consider the following. "Croats and Muslims have never fought for Yugoslavia, except episodically. And after wars, they have always devoted themselves to the destruction of Yugoslavia. "(B) In both previous wars they are on the side of the aggressor, and in this war they are relying on extremist emigrants. Pro-Germanic countries and Islamic countries have embarked on the breakup of Yugoslavia and Serbdom which has been made possible by the internal decay of the political and military establishment of the former SFRY. The goal of Croats and Muslims is not a union with us tomorrow --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, you should slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My excuse. "The goal of Croats and Muslims is not a union with us tomorrow, but to use cunning and international pressure to achieve the establishment of a greater Croatia within its historical borders, or to Islamise Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, again, is it not true that the ERS and the VRS leadership acted very much in their own interests when think agreed to co-operate with the HVO and that there were no altruistic motives whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The statement you read out may be a personal opinion on the part of General Mladic, but it is based on historical facts. Let me remind you that the first person who launched resistance in the former Yugoslavia Josip Broz Tito, who was a Croat. Many Croats and Muslims were killed fighting for the anti-fascist coalition, much the same way as there were many Serbs who fought for the Axis forces. As for his opinion about the destruction of Yugoslavia, that's his own view. In terms of whether they worked in the interests of Yugoslavia, absolutely so. There would not have been any conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Travnik had there not been for the VRS which, from Bosanska Krajina, kept sending civilians via Vlasic and ending up with the figure of 17.600. Of course, it was one of the reasons which contributed to the conflict of Muslims and Croats in Travnik. According to the laws of physics, the chain breaks at its weakest link, the weakest link being the Croatian locations in Central Bosnia. When the Muslims could no longer oppose the Serbs militarily, they turned on Croats when fighting for territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention to another paragraph here in this document which is -- it's -- it's the second-but-last paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So if we can move to the -- to the next page of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I'll read out again this paragraph to you. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do so, may I ask you what the term "ERS" means, which you used on line 25, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Oh did I -- I meant "RS", the Republika Srpska, rather than ERS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. So if we can move to the last page of this document. It's on page 3 in the English version and also page 3 on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I'll read out -- this is paragraph which starts: "Members of the 1st KK." "Members of the 1st KK and the 1st KK command deserve great credit for the results achieved so far. In respect of the above noted matters relating to the evacuation of the Croats from Travnik, the international public took this as the biggest Croatian defeat in this war and so the total downfall of Croats and the defeat of the Muslims should be effected along those lines." Sir, did you realise that when the VRS offered their assistance in the evacuation of the Bosnian Croats from Travnik, General Mladic's primary intention was the total downfall of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were at least three warring parties, even if we take into account the war between Muslims and Muslims. Of course, every party wanted to militarily defeat the other side completely and there's nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 65 ter 00925 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00925 receives Exhibit P7094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Bos. The document is admitted into evidence and it's been given a number, so P7094.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, did you know that a number of Bosnian Croat civilians who fled the Serb-controlled areas in Travnik in 1993 became part of an exchange agreement by which Serb civilians from Livno and Tomislavgrad were to be released by the HVO? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that when I was exchanged in Baras. At the command of the brigade there, I saw a document signed by the chief of the intelligence and security, Mr. Kesa Ratko, and I believe already on the 8th of September an agreement had been reached and our fate had been decided even as we arrived at Manjaca, although we didn't know it then. I later learned about it by looking at documents that had been sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at two of these documents which talk about this exchange agreement and let's see if we talk about the same agreement here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 31929 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The previous date was not 8th September but the 8th or 9th November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe just to clarify the date which the interpreter has just...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you were talking about earlier that your fate had been decided upon, you mentioned the date of 8th September. Is that the date -- or 8 November? Which exact date were you --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in June or in July, when we had already been transported to Manjaca. Not September. In September, I was already in Kiseljak. It was the 8th of June. I think. I think. Take it with a grain of salt. It was 22 years ago. My memory is not as fresh as it used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that makes sense, 8 of June. Sir, we're now looking at a document which is an HVO intelligence report dated the 19th of June, 1993, and under the heading "Tomislavgrad Sector," the second paragraph reads: "At the negotiations in Celebic, representatives of the Serb side offered 1789 civilians from the Lasva area for exchange, 500 of them children, 471 men eligible for military services [sic] which the Serbs deemed to be HVO soldiers, and 29 wounded HVO members who are located in hospital in Banja Luka. In return, they are seeking that all civilians of Serb ethnicity from Rascani (outside Tomislavgrad) and the Livno municipality, as well as Soldier RS who strayed onto our territory, and two other SRNA, Bosnian Serb radio and news agency journalists, who were taken prisoner near the Peruca dam be released." Sir is this the exchange agreements which you have been referring to as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I believe this is about an exchange of people after we were exchanged. Because we later reached the territory controlled by the VRS from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not talking about the exchange that you have may have been involved, but I'm talking here about Bosnian Croat civilians who -- yeah, who have -- who have -- who were moved to Croatia, this group of 1.789 civilians. Let me look -- let's look at one other document on -- on this particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could the Registry bring up 65 ter 31930.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, here on the screen, we see, this is an order signed by HVO President Jadranko Prlic and co-signed by the head of the defence department Bruno Stojicic and the head of the department of internal affairs, Branko Kvesic. The order is addressed to the HVO Livno and Tomislavgrad, and it's dated the 26th of June 1993, a week later from that first report we saw. Now, in this order we can see that the HVO actually complied with the proposed exchange agreement, as they ordered the HVO authorities in Livno and Tomislavgrad, and I read it out: "With regards to the agreement on exchange of detainees and release of civilians ... to ensure an unobstructed departure of all members of Serbian people from the areas of these municipality [sic] (this pertains to those who wish to do so) to the territory under Serb control." Sir, would you agree with me that through this order the HVO actually complied with their part of the exchange agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't comment on this agreement because I still believe that it's an agreement that concerns refugees from the Novi Travnik area, perhaps even Bugojno at this time, after our withdrawal from Travnik. Very soon after, part of the HVO forces and civilians from Travnik also left, and even those from Bugojno. I believe there was not one integral agreement. At this time, all the civilians and conscripts from the area of Travnik had already been exchanged. I don't think there was agreement on this issue because after that document signed by the military and intelligence security chief Mr. Pjesa or Kesa, there must have been something else. But what agreement and at what level, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 65 ter 31929 and 31930 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31929 receives Exhibit P7095, Your Honours. Document 31930 receives Exhibit P7096, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Both 31929 is admitted into evidence under that number, and 31930 is also admitted as P7096. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kolenda, I want to continue talking about the VRS motive for assisting the HVO evacuation. Did you know that the HVO actually had to pay for the VRS assistance in the evacuation of the Bosnian Croats from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And let me ask the Registry to bring up Rule 65 ter 00995. I think I've -- the correct reference should have been 955, rather than 995. I'm sorry. So it's 65 ter 955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the form that was earlier on --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the screen was correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now it has disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, it's -- I think the correct number was 995. My apologies. I think ... so we'll have to get back to 995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, we're looking at here at a -- another communication from General Mladic, and I hope you can read it. It's -- the B/C/S version is not very clear. I don't know if we need to enlarge it, but let me read out to you the first paragraph of this communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, I'm ... this is not the correct document. No, it is, I'm sorry. It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Starting in the first paragraph, the second line, and I'll read it out: "The HVO will deliver you a package in which there should be 1 million, 500.000 deutschemark or other hard currency in the same quantity. The money is meant for paying food supply and other services related to the transportation of the Croatian civilians from the Central Bosnia, Travnik, and Vares region (food, fuel, transportation, cigarettes and such)." Sir, were you aware that the HVO paid money to cover the cost of the VRS assistance in the evacuation of the Bosnian Croat civilians in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to admit 65 ter 00995 into evidence -- tender into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00995 receives Exhibit P7097, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted as P7097. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Kolenda, is it correct that after the fall of Travnik the VRS and the HVO continued to co-operate in the war against the ABiH in Central Bosnia in the summer and autumn of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the area of the Lasva valley, then, no, because they had no points of contact. In the area of Kiseljak and Zepca area, they did have a close co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. And isn't it true that the VRS used the HVO army to their advantage in military operations against the ABiH forces who often had many more soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say anything about this. In the case of the Travnik conflict, a couple of times they gave us artillery support at the request of our brigade command. As for close military co-operation, I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you one more document, which is 65 ter 00984. Now, sir, this is a document -- this document is a report from the HVO Kiseljak Brigade and it's addressed to the HVO Main Staff and it's dated the 6th of July 1993, and it talks about HVO's contact and further co-operation with the XY side which, from the context of this document, seems to be a reference to the Serb side. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment because in that period I had only just arrived in Kiseljak and I was not at the brigade command. I was at the police command. But that there was close co-operation between these two sides in the exchange of goods such as oil, fuel, and ammunition, I saw that for myself. Only on the 4th of December was I appointed legal advisor in the Josip Jelacic Brigade. I don't know what happened before that, but as a deputy police commander I had my own area of responsibility vis-à-vis the Muslims in the area of Tarcin; that is to say, facing the Tarcin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in this document HVO Kiseljak reports on the outcome of a meeting organised by the VRS in which delivery of VRS equipment and artillery support was discussed. And as we can see in paragraph 1, there is a Serb proposal for a meeting between the HVO General Petkovic and General Mladic. And in the information under item 2 reads, and I'll read that out to you: "That our total unpaid debt, according to their calculation, delivered equipment and artillery support - amounts to 5.700.000 and that General Mladic has all the information about that. I do not know exactly how they explain this large sum of money but for your information we have enclosed the specification of all equipment that has been taken over and the invoices for the deposited money that we gave to them, and you also received the price list, which they offered to us." Now the report then continues to talk about equipment and artillery that the HVO Kiseljak Brigade is still in need of. And if we can then maybe move to the next page of this document, we see under -- in the bottom under "attachment" there's a list of -- of -- of equipment. It starts with 6.9-millimetre bullets. Quantity, 4.099, 500, and so on. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, are you not allowed to talk aloud in court. You do know that. Sorry, Mr. Bos. You said it starts with 6.9. I'm trying to look for 6.9. I can't see it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah, apologies. It's 7.9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I misread it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So there is a whole list of equipment and if we can then -- and artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And if we could then move to the last page of this document, where this list continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: There we can read at the end, it reads: "The HVO had already deposited a total amount of 1.191.246 in cash and two D-2 fuel trucks with ten metric tonnes of fuel each." Sir, were you aware that the equipment and artillery support that the VRS offered the HVO in their armed struggle against the ABiH in Central Bosnia in the summer and autumn of 1993 came with a very serious price tag for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this document, but I know what was going on on the ground in this area. When I came to the area of Kiseljak, Krasulje, and Vojnica, I saw a weapon that we called Praga. It's a cannon with multiple barrels. I'm not an expert. But I know that stories went around that more than a million deutschemark had been paid to the Serbs for it. As for trade, there was constant trade. Serbs needed fuel and the Croats needed weapons and ammunition. There were interest groups on both sides who easily found a common language. You know what war is like. Thieves and outlaws come to the surface and dominate, more or less. I know that medical assistance for one HVO soldier was once paid 2.000 deutschemark. Some of this money probably went into private pockets. As for trade in fuel and weaponry, that went on throughout the war, not only in Kiseljak. It was also in Zepca, in any other area. It was not a war motivated by pure patriotism, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I tender Exhibit 65 ter 00984 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00984 receives Exhibit P7098, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And this concludes my cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bos. Mr. Lukic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. I have several questions. I probably will need the break to consult with my client regarding at least two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want us to take a break now, preferably?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I, just for the record, clarify that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, please stop talking aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, three words are missing on the record, the words spoken by the Presiding Judge, "the document is received."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted, yes. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, you were saying something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would preferably take an early break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, we're going to take a break for 20 minutes. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter 20. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kolenda, yet again, on another day.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I won't take long.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page one of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you discussed the payment for ammunition, which is not in dispute, I wanted to ask you whether, however, you knew anything specific about this document or about this operation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that General Petkovic met with General Mladic on the 7th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Lukic mentioned the name of a hotel in the question that we did not catch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Plaza. The name of the hotel is Plaza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you mentioned the name which the interpreters did not catch, the name of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is Hotel Plaza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Hotel Plaza.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have P709, please. Actually, 7093. [In English] If we can enlarge B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, Mr. Kolenda, it is recorded that you spoke with someone from Glas Srpski. It was published on the 15th of June, 1992. In the last paragraph, the first sentence reads: "The conflict between Muslims and Croats in Travnik has been going on for sometime. It all began nine months ago with the murder of Ivica Stojak. Although it is known who and how killed him, not even an investigation was launched." Mr. Kolenda, what was the ethnic background of the person who was killed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat and he used to command a HVO brigade in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who killed him? What were you trying to insinuate?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't insinuating. What happened was that there was a temporary check-point set up by Muslim forces. They were commanded by a certain Mr. Terzic. From the check-point, fire was opened at the delegation, including Mr. Stojak and Mr. Gaso. Mr. Stojak was killed and Mr. Gaso was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next you mentioned the number of refugees pumped into Travnik. You say there were four brigades of the ABiH in Travnik. Was one of those brigades established in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what formation it was, but in late 1992 there was a unit that came from Croatia to Travnik. It was headed by Colonel Alagic and his assistant, Major Cuskic. They had been trained and equipped in Croatia and placed in the Travnik barracks. It definitely created an imbalance of forces in Travnik. With the sending of the refugees from the Vlasic plateau to Travnik, and the latest information I had at the time in early June there were 17.600 of them, as that was happening, they were recruiting all military-aged men placing them in the barracks. They used them to set up another two brigades, the Banja Luka or Krajina Brigade, something of the sort. The Muslims in Travnik on top of those brigades had at least another two brigades comprising military-aged men who had been refugees from the Bosnian Krajina. That put the ratio of 8:1 in favour of the Muslims, when compared to the HVO. In a military sense, the western part of Travnik was lost even back then, and the conflict that erupted six or seven months later simply confirmed that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last page on -- the last sentence on this page reads: "Over the past two months, after they completed the expulsions of Serbs at least 100 Croat families have been expelled from their homes in Travnik." Who was expelling the Serbs and Croats from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there are over 17.000 refugees in Travnik itself, and even more in Zenica and Bugojno and elsewhere, and as they were creating brigades from those newly arrived conscripts, in the first half of 1993 they mainly waged war along the Sarajevo corridor trying to break through. I think that many were killed at the front lines in Cekrcici. Such people would then return to Travnik wounded and traumatised, causing incidents. They wanted to find better accommodation for their families to get them out of collection centres. That is why they were much pressure put on people occupying apartments in Travnik, especially on Serb families. There was constant pressure to have them moved out, expelled, in order to occupy their apartments and seize their property. As for the 100 Croat -- Croats referred here, it probably had to do with the people at the beginning of the conflict. They were from the area where the Muslim forces had taken territory and they were then expelled to the western part of Travnik where our brigade had control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, you have spoken now for the last three minutes. The question to you was who expelled the Serbs and Croats from Travnik, and in all that long speech that you gave you haven't answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the answer to the question. That's all. Not this whole paragraph that you told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for your caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please control the witness, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now focus on the day when you left Travnik. What happened with the HVO unit from the village of Bikosa?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Bikosa is actually a hamlet in the area of Guca Gora and Malin. After an attack by a Muslim brigade, some 20 fighters withdrew but the civilians were captured. The soldiers were then blackmailed with returning and surrendering so as not to see their civilians killed. When they surrendered, they put them in front of a firing squad and killed 18 of them. One managed to escape and join us at Vlasic. He lived to tell us the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some people remained in the town itself, such as four ministers, Ivo Rajkovic, Ivo Fisic, the minister of trade, the local pastor, the Deputy Police Commander Popovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you lead, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We haven't heard about this evidence from this witness and you are telling it for the first time. Don't even know whether it arises from cross-examination. I don't know whether Mr. Bos can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just then ask what happened with people who stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kolenda, what happened with the people who remained in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the way developments took place, we failed to evacuate some Croats from Travnik. We believe there were between 2-and-a-half- and 3.000, including a number of government officials from the HVO and the Travnik government, including Minister Fisic and the late Minister Rajkovic. After a while, after they had to sweep streets and after they were humiliated, they were kidnapped and taken to the village of Mehoric. My friend who was assistant commander of the war time police - he was the second in command while I was the first in command - well, in any case he was beheaded in a ritual, and the other captured had to kiss that head. After two or three months of beatings, following an army intervention they were released or exchanged, and there is proof of that in the book of my dear late friend, Professor Rajkovic. It was quite dramatic with a lot of horrifying incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Immediately prior to your departure from Travnik, your segment of the armed forces was the enemy of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: En route and when accommodation was found for you through Serb territory, were any Croats killed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The civilians who reached Croatia, was it something they wanted themselves? In other words, did you ask the Serb component to release the civilians in order to reach Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the Croatian component was withdrawing from Travnik, were the Muslims trying to take up former Croatian positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us look at P3683 briefly - you have been shown that document before - from the Main Staff of the VRS dated the 7th of June, 1993. This document describes the treatment of HVO members and Croatian civilian population. Does it mainly reflect what had previously been agreed with -- agreed upon with the Serb side? For example, item 1, it says: "Have the civilians transferred to Croatia to the area of Novska with the assistance of the ICRC"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One does need to say that it happened only after we had been taken to Manjaca, but in any case the procedure was followed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 2, it says that the persons fit for military service and HVO units' members should be accommodated at Manjaca. When were you told this; and did you agree to it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a matter of agreeing to it or not. We could either stay or take it. When we were in the area of Vlasic, in Galica, we were told that we would be transported to Manjaca after we were separated from the civilians. It included the men who were of military age. I have to say that not all of them were soldiers and policemen though. It wasn't a matter of choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that some socially owned vehicles were requisitioned. Did you continue on foot or were you driven to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some military trucks arrived and the people were put on those trucks; the men who were of military age. That is how we were transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Item 4 states: "People in private vehicles with their private belongings should be released as part of the ICRC convoy in order to leave our territory." With the exception of the one seized vehicle, the jeep you mentioned, did the rest continue their travel and join the ICRC convoy in order to reach Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the one vehicle because I know about it. The rest continued. I really don't know whether there were any other vehicles that remained behind. I was no longer in the area. In any case, my official vehicle reached Croatia without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the next page in B/C/S, item 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Item 6 is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we also need the next page for the second part. [In English] But we need the second part in English, so we need next page, and we need the next page in B/C/S as well. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says persons who are found through intelligence vetting to have committed crimes against the Serb population in the period up to the liberation of Jajce and the Vlasic plateau are to be separated and criminal proceedings instituted. The question is was any separated from your group, or did the entire group arrive from Manjaca to Croat-controlled territory near Vares?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were at Manjaca, one day the command of the VRS asked that unit commanders in Manjaca be brought and interrogated. I know about this only from what they told me, because I was brought later. None of them were abused, they were questioned as to who they were, which rank they held, et cetera. However, apart from 20 Serbs who were able-bodied men of military age, there were 880 people who chose to stay at Manjaca or later went to join the VRS or reunite with their families. But among us - what I'm trying to say - were not only Croats, there were some Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honours. I think I'm close to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, thank you very much for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing comes up, Mr. Bos?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Kolenda, this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony at the Tribunal. Just to thank you very much for coming all the way to the Tribunal to come and give your evidence and to answer the questions asked by everybody. You may now leave the courtroom and go home, but please travel well back home. You may follow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may follow the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we call the next witness, there are a few issues that we'd like to deal with. The first one relates to the testimony of Vojislav Krsic, and that relates to Exhibit P851. On the 4th of December 2014 and during cross-examination of Vojislav Krsic, an issue arose with the word "nationality" in the English translation of Exhibit P851. And this can be found at transcript pages 29315 and 29316. On the 18th of December the Prosecution informed the Chamber via e-mail that a revised English translation of Exhibit P851 had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0129-3842-A-ET. Does the Defence have any objection to this translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We -- can you replace it then. We haven't checked it yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We'll do that. Then the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current translation of P851 with the revised translation. And if the Defence has any comments to make, they are welcome to do so later. The next issue relates to the remaining issue from the testimony of Cedo Sipovac and relates to Exhibits D767, D768, and D769. On the 12th of November, 2014, again during examination-in-chief of Cedo Sipovac, these exhibits - D767, D768, and D769 - were marked for identification pending translation. At that time the Defence stated that another once would discuss these documents in more detail. This can be found at transcript page 28220. On the 21st of January, 2015, the Defence informed the Chamber via e-mail that the English translations have been uploaded into e-court under the following document ID numbers: ID 19-0739 for document D767.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I said ID. It's 1D. It's 1D19-0739 for document D767. 1D19-0983 for document D768. And 1D19-0997 for document D769. As the translation issues are resolved, the remaining issue seems to be whether the Defence still wants to tender the three documents through Witness Cedo Sipovac rather than through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since Cedo Sipovac testified about these documents, Your Honour, we would tender through him as well, and we would probably use with another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is the Prosecution still saying that it has no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually -- actually, Your Honour, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'd communicated to the Defence by e-mail on January 22nd that we did object to them being introduced through Mr. Sipovac and had been expecting the Defence to use them with another witness as they'd said at the time and invited the Defence to discuss the matter with us in the same communication. So we maintain our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You maintain your objections. Well, Mr. Lukic, you've got then to decide are going to argue the objection or are you going to tender these documents through another witness later? You make up your mind. You don't have to answer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll then have your proposal to respond later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Good morning, Mr. Pasic. I hope you are Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to you, and I'm terribly sorry to keep you waiting while we were attending to other matters. Mr. Pasic, you -- can you please make the declaration that -- a copy of which is handed to you before you make your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You may now be seated. Mr. Pasic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic -- by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I may be excused from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who is replacing you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, are you sufficiently visible and can you see us from that angle?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're certainly sufficiently visible, Your Honour. If I'm sufficiently visible to you, then I'm satisfied to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would first call Mr. Pasic's statement on our screens. It's 1D4766a.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, would you slowly tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Radomir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you give a written statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll need paragraph 47 from this statement. That's page 15 in B/C/S and 19 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, Mr. Pasic, you talk about the surrender of weapons and the deadline for surrendering them. You told me the date of 10 May was a mistake, that it should be 11th May.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a mistake. I think the deadline was 10 May -- sorry, 11 May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 49 and paragraph 50, we should compare. In the second paragraph of 49, in the second sentence, you say: "I think there was no shelling whatsoever." And in paragraph 50, the second passage, you say: "But I've already said that there was no shelling except in some places where there was resistance, and I believe that the weapon used was of a lighter calibre, but there was no heavy artillery as far as I know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the English at that part says something completely different. It says: "And I think that the weapon carried kind of shelling, but heavily artillery as far as I every known did not exist."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. In the Karadzic trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have to go to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: English version is, I think, authoritative, since they submitted English statements. So I would then go with the English version, whatever it says in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Whatever you do, can you also explain why the witness keeps saying "I was explained," and in particular, in paragraph 47, he says: "I was explained that around the 9th of May, 1992, a Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff under Radomir Pasic," now, he is Radomir Pasic, "issued an ultimatum over Bosanski Novi." He either knows he issued it. It cannot be explained to him, if he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, obviously Karadzic's Defence had this habit to start explaining adjudicated facts with the -- since the adjudicated facts are different in our case, we redacted that adjudicated fact. So that's -- they also started with "I was explained." They wanted to say that the witness was introduced to adjudicated fact that he was supposed to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hmm. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we submitted Karadzic's statement, so we are now stuck with the formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are indeed stuck. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, but just in the interest of accuracy. I'm not certain what is intended by the expression that the English versions are authoritative because the Karadzic Defence team submitted those. In fact, as the Court would be aware from the typical practice involving most witnesses, but obviously not English-speaking witnesses, the communication was in Serbian. The witness often signed a Serbian version which was translated into English. If discrepancies arose in that context, recourse was had to presumably both documents to make sure they adequately conformed, but I at least at this moment can't recall a point at which the -- the -- such a matter, if it arose, was resolved by asserting that the English version was authoritative if, in fact, it was the Serbian version which the witness could read and read only and which the witnesses had signed. That, I don't think, would make particular sense in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, your very last sentence is the very important part. This statement here, the version that is signed, is the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the English is not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly. In this case, yes. But we were informed by Karadzic's Defence members that they would actually give usually English version to witnesses to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, sure. It's -- the position you are taking, that in this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the English version is authoritative, that's not correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not correct, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- because that's not the one signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I trust, of course, Mr. Tieger. He was part of Karadzic's trial. I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Tieger would be interested in testifying about things that happened in the Karadzic case, but in the -- and then again, of course, we have got Mr. Traldi here who is steering the Prosecution's ship.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't think that's -- I think that's giving me far too much credit, Your Honour. But for this particular cross, it would be useful to have in English, if the Defence isn't considering the English version of that paragraph authoritative, it would be useful to have it corrected orally so that we have on the transcript or on the record in some way, for those of us that don't read Serbian, what the witness's evidence on that point is. And I think it was the end of paragraph 50 that was at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. So as you make corrections, can you attend to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would ask, actually, the witness, so he tells us what actually is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Pasic, could you tell us today about what you know. Was there no shelling whatsoever; was there shelling from heavy weaponry; was there shelling from lighter weaponry? What is it that you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go into the technical aspects. I know what statement I gave in the Serbian version, and I stand behind what I said, never mind whether it was two, five, or ten years ago. But I must say there was a debate at that time as to the meaning of shelling. I did serve in the army, and maybe I don't have an accurate definition of shelling, but I will repeat before this Court that there was no shelling, in my understanding of the word, for the simple reason that in that period the Territorial Defence, which was the only official military body, if I can put it that way, had no heavy artillery, and by "heavy artillery," I mean a large-calibre cannons, rocket systems, et cetera. The Territorial Defence had light infantry weapons, and I'm trying to be precise in my terminology. In terms of artillery, they had mortars. Smaller ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I think you have explained yourself. Thank you very much. You have explained yourself. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if we can have the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the screen before you, do you see the signature, Mr. Pasic? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's my signature. 5 July 2013; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is it the case that my colleagues from the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic correctly wrote in this statement all that you've told them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Taking into account the few corrections you made.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I saw was completely accurate and identical to what I said in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this statement reflect the truth, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: All that I said was the truth and for the purpose of getting at the truth, and I talked only about things I had direct knowledge of or was directly involved in. So I gave my statement only about things that I remember and know about. Maybe I've omitted certain things because I forgot them, but I remember and I know what I said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put you to the same questions today, would you answer the same, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. It would not be the same word for word, but substantially it would be the same. I couldn't answer otherwise because I know nothing else, nothing different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should now tendered Mr. Pasic's statement, 1D4766a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we can admit it, Mr. Lukic, you asked the witness to explain paragraph 50 and he went on into a very long explanation. Can you, in very precise terms, telling us what must be changed, if anything at all, in paragraph 50 as it stands, and if so, replaced with what wording? Just a short -- just that short part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we get that part of the statement back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If the statement can be brought on the screen. It's paragraph 50 of the witness's statement, which is 1D4766a.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I wouldn't actually change anything in paragraph 50. I would change paragraph 59 [sic], when it says that there was no shelling at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the problem is when you read out paragraph 50 from the B/C/S, I told you it does not correspond with what we read on paragraph 50 in the English. So you got to tell us what the correct thing is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I would read that portion of paragraph 50 and ask the translators, if possible to translate it. I will read slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. That is the last sentence of paragraph 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in English. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, just to be very clear, you said on -- in line 11, page 38: "I would change paragraph 59, when it says there was no shelling at all."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you really refer to 59 or to 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 49, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because were recorded as having said "59," but we agree you mean 49?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Your Honour. Thank you. I will read last two sentences in B/C/S so we don't miss anything, or maybe I should read the whole paragraph in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... last sentence. But if you want to read the last two sentences, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] "So that this former TO Staff was reformulated into the Army of the Republika Srpska of Bosnia-Herzegovina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I stop you. Which paragraph are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm reading paragraph 50, second paragraph from paragraph 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you starting the whole paragraph in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In last two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The word "reformulated" here makes no sense in either Serbian or English. We have difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... but I've already said there had been no shelling except in certain places where there had been resistance, and I believe that this kind of shelling was from some light weaponry; but, to the best of my knowledge, there was no heavy artillery."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we should change paragraph 49, one sentence in the second paragraph of paragraph 49. In the second line, there was a sentence in English: "I think that there was no shelling." The same sentence we can find in B/C/S, and it should read: "I think there was only shelling from light" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should read it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] "And I believe the shelling was only from infantry weapons, such as light mortars ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the problem now is that the witness attested to the text before it was changed by you now. So perhaps you can put one question to the witness if that -- all that covers -- his attestation covers even the changes made now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, following this correction, as I read it out, the rest of your statement, was it accurately recorded to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Everything recorded in my statement is truthful. If this was a point of dispute, perhaps it would be good for a military expert to precisely define the concept of shelling. I don't know whether I was understood or if the interpreters correctly interpreted but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you. Mr. Pasic, can I ask you to please listen carefully to the questions that are put to you. Answer that question and that question only. We know that you've got lots to tell us, but we don't have the time to listen to everything that you may want to tell us. So listen clearly and stop after answering the question, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, you should reformulate your question: Not referring to the rest of your statement but that portions in paragraph 49 and 50 you have changed or read in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, because of the attestation, I have to ask you this: Paragraphs 49 and 50, are they now correctly entered in the statement, following the corrections we just made, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I can't answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can't answer request with a yes or no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're obviously trying to confuse me. I don't know what your intent is. I understand that you have to time constraints, but have you to understand me. I came here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you came here to tell the truth, sir. But you didn't come here voluntarily, you were asked to come here. And if those who called you to come here have specific questions to put to you, they don't want to listen to all the story that you want to tell, so you are going to answer the questions that are put to you by those people, that and that only. Is that clear to you? Because they are the people who called you here and they know what they want from you. You don't know what they want from you, okay? Put the question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, please. This is important to have your statement admitted. The way I read out the sentence from paragraph 49 which also corresponds with what is recorded in paragraph 50, does it reflect what you know? If it doesn't, tell us, and we can continue correcting.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I don't see what's in dispute here. I said that there was no shelling, and I specified in these paragraphs what I understood under the term "shelling." I repeat, I'm not a military expert. I need to repeat: If one understands shelling as using light weaponry, then there was shelling. If not, then there was no shelling. So in terms of terminology, I would like someone to define the concept of shelling to me in order to be able to answer. I think I'm making myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please control your witness. Let him answer the questions that you are putting. Given the answer that he has given, he's obviously refusing to attest to his statement and therefore it cannot be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you understand what you are doing now? Do you not want to have your statement admitted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: No, I am not withdrawing anything. I'm simply trying to say that I do stand by my statement. I guess the translation was wrong. I stand by my statement. Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just -- let me just let you know something. You know, we work on certain procedures in this place and you probably may not have knowledge of how we work. Now, Mr. Lukic is asking you a question which needs to be answered "yes" or "no" if this statement of yours must go into court. And if you keep giving these explanations, that you are not a military expert, you are not answering the question that is being put to you, and that will result in your statement and your evidence not being taken into consideration in this case. So I ask you for the last time, on behalf of Mr. Lukic, do you accept -- do you confirm, rather, that the corrections made to paragraph 49 and paragraph 50 as read out to you correctly reflect your statement? And you're going to answer me "yes" or "no." Anything else, I'm going to stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will redact his statement. I will redact paragraph 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He hasn't confirmed the statement, so it cannot be admitted. He's refusing to admit it -- he is refusing to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood the witness correctly, he confirms that the B/C/S version is correct but there's a translation issue. We can't check that because if that is a translation issue, then we need a new translation of the B/C/S. But we don't know that, and therefore at the moment the basis for admission is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can we make -- it has never happened to me. I was being practicing in front of this Tribunal for 15 years and this is the first time that my witness is refusing to attest his own statement. So can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So have we.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to maybe regroup myself, and can we have a ten-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ten-minute break. Well, it's time for a normal break. We'll take our normal break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you may follow the usher. We are going to take a short break for 20 minutes. We'll call you later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take a break and come back at ten past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- I beg your pardon. May the witness please be called -- brought into the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to reformulate once more, and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasic, let's try another time. The rest of the statement seems to be fine. We need to see what happens with paragraph 49. We found small differences between 49 and 50, and we have to reconcile these. We left paragraph 50 as recorded in the Serbian language, or in the B/C/S. I will read out the disputed sentence in paragraph 49, and I have a new suggestion. Perhaps then you can agree on the formulation. I may have been insufficiently clear last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just for the record to be clear, it's not a disputed portion. It's a correction to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Correction to be made, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He does think there is a dispute and there is no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I suggest the following correction: I would leave the sentence as is and add "forwards" in the B/C/S. Please follow it on the screen as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: Could you enlarge a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Last paragraph on this B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kindly enlarge even further. I can't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can remove the English one because we have it in a hard copy before us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second row of the last paragraph, it reads: "I also think that there was no shelling." The corrected version should be formulated as follows, if you agree: "And I think that there was no shelling from heavy artillery weapons."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Following this correction, is the rest of paragraph 49 exactly what you want it to say in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I agree. I apologise if I created a problem. That was not my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would it be proper now to offer this statement into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's fine. Has confirmed now the whole statement as corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The statement is admitted into evidence. It is 1D4766a. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D04766a receives Exhibit D890, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise if I caused problems for you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC
utterances.text: I apologise to all of you as well.
